etymology: From the Greek panoplia, “full armour” or “the complete equipment of a soldier,” the apostle’s figure for the believer’s defence in spiritual warfare.
biblical_def: The whole armour of God is the apostle Paul’s great figure for the believer’s defence against the powers of darkness, set out at the close of the epistle to the Ephesians. Put on the whole armour of God, he writes, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil (Eph 6:11); for we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places (Eph 6:12). The dictionary marks the warfare as wholly spiritual: the Christian’s enemies are not men but devils, and his weapons are not carnal. The armour is God’s armour, not the soldier’s own; it is grace wrought in him and furnished to him, that he may withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand (Eph 6:13). So the Scripture teaches that the saint stands not by his native strength but by the armour his Lord supplies, and that the whole panoply must be taken, for a single piece neglected leaves an opening for the adversary. The pieces that follow — the girdle of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the shoes of the gospel, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the sword of the Spirit — are not the soldier’s invention but the grace of God given for his keeping, that he who is feeble in himself may be strong in the Lord, and in the power of His might (Eph 6:10).
webster_summary: The complete spiritual armour God furnishes the believer, that he may stand against the devil in the evil day.

etymology: From the Greek aletheia, “truth” or “reality,” the first piece of the believer’s armour, figured as the soldier’s girdle that binds and braces him for battle.
biblical_def: The girdle of truth is the first piece of the whole armour of God, the belt that the apostle bids the believer fasten before all the rest: Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth (Eph 6:14). In the ancient warfare the soldier girded up his flowing garments with a stout belt before he could fight or run, that nothing might hinder or entangle him; and so the girdle stands first, for it braces the whole man and holds the other pieces in their place. The dictionary marks the girdle as the truth of God laid hold of and lived in — both the truth of doctrine, the faithful word, and the truth of an upright and unfeigned heart, the inward integrity that answers to it. The Christian who would stand must first be girt with truth, knowing the word of God as it is and walking in sincerity before Him; for a man double in heart, or loose and uncertain in what he believes, is undone before the fight begins. So the Scripture teaches that the loins of the mind must be girded up (1Pe 1:13), and that the LORD desireth truth in the inward parts (Psa 51:6). Christ Himself is the truth (Joh 14:6), and the saint girded with Him stands braced and ready, his garments gathered up, no part of him left loose for the adversary to seize, that he may withstand in the evil day.
webster_summary: The first piece of the armour, the truth of God and uprightness of heart that braces the believer for battle.

etymology: From the Greek thorax, “breastplate” or “corselet,” the second piece of the armour, figuring the righteousness that guards the believer’s heart in battle.
biblical_def: The breastplate of righteousness is the second piece of the whole armour of God, the corselet that the apostle bids the believer put on to guard his vital parts: having on the breastplate of righteousness (Eph 6:14). As the soldier’s breastplate covered his heart and bowels against the thrust of the sword, so righteousness guards the believer’s heart against the assaults of the devil, who is the accuser of the brethren (Rev 12:10). The dictionary marks a twofold righteousness in this breastplate. First and foremost is the imputed righteousness of Christ, that perfect obedience reckoned to the believer by faith, by which he is made the righteousness of God in Him (2Co 5:21); this is the breastplate that turns away every accusation, for who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth (Rom 8:33). Second is the practical righteousness wrought in the saint by the Spirit, the holy walk and good conscience that leave the adversary no foothold. The two are never sundered: the imputed righteousness of Christ is the ground of the believer’s standing, and the practical righteousness of a holy life is its fruit. So the Scripture teaches that the heart guarded by Christ’s righteousness imputed, and adorned with righteousness practised, stands secure against the accusations of the wicked one; for the breastplate is not the soldier’s own merit but the gift of God in Christ.
webster_summary: The second piece of the armour, Christ’s imputed righteousness and the saint’s holy walk, guarding the heart in battle.

etymology: From the Greek hetoimasia, “preparation” or “readiness,” the third piece of the armour, figuring the gospel of peace as the soldier’s sandals that make him sure-footed for the march.
biblical_def: The shoes of the gospel are the third piece of the whole armour of God, the sandals that shod the believer’s feet for the battle: and your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace (Eph 6:15). As the soldier could neither stand firm nor march without his sandals, so the believer needs his feet made ready by the gospel. The dictionary marks this readiness in a twofold sense. It is the firm footing the gospel of peace gives, that a man reconciled to God stands fast and is not moved; being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom 5:1), and that peace steadies him in every assault. And it is a readiness to publish that peace, after the manner of the messenger whose feet are beautiful upon the mountains: how beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things (Rom 10:15). So the Scripture teaches that the gospel of peace both grounds the saint and sends him: it gives him a sure footing within, that he stands unshaken, and a ready foot without, that he follow his Captain and carry the glad tidings to others. The man shod with the gospel is at peace with God through Christ, and therefore neither slips in the battle nor draws back from the march.
webster_summary: The third piece of the armour, the gospel of peace that grounds the believer and makes him ready to march and to publish it.

etymology: From the Greek thureos, the large door-shaped shield that covered the whole body, the fourth piece of the armour, figuring faith as the believer’s great defence against the darts of the wicked.
biblical_def: The shield of faith is the fourth piece of the whole armour of God, and the apostle sets it above all the rest: above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked (Eph 6:16). The shield he names is the great door-shaped buckler that covered the whole soldier from head to foot, behind which he might shelter his whole body; and the fiery darts are the burning arrows of the adversary — his temptations, his blasphemous suggestions, his accusations and despairing thoughts shot flaming into the soul. The dictionary marks faith as the believer’s shield, for faith lays hold on Christ and His promises, and behind that shield every fiery dart is caught and quenched. It is not the strength of the believer’s faith in itself, but the worth of the Christ whom faith grasps, that quenches the darts; faith holds up between the soul and the enemy the finished work and sure word of God, and the burning arrow falls dead against it. So the Scripture teaches that this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith (1Jo 5:4), and the just shall live by his faith (Hab 2:4). The shield is set above the rest because it guards the whole man; the saint who lifts it, hiding behind Christ and trusting the promise, finds not one flaming dart can pierce to wound the soul.

etymology: From the Greek perikephalaia, “that which is about the head,” the helmet, the fifth piece of the armour, figuring the hope of salvation that guards the believer’s mind.
biblical_def: The helmet of salvation is the fifth piece of the whole armour of God: And take the helmet of salvation (Eph 6:17). As the helmet guarded the soldier’s head, the seat of life and thought, so the assurance and hope of salvation guard the believer’s mind against the despairing and doubting thoughts the adversary would lodge there. The apostle opens the figure more fully in another place, where he bids the saints take for an helmet, the hope of salvation (1Th 5:8); for it is the sure hope of final deliverance, the confident expectation of glory laid up in Christ, that keeps the head erect and the mind steadfast in the fight. The dictionary marks this helmet as the believer’s assurance: not a hope that may fail, but a lively hope grounded on the finished work of Christ and the faithfulness of God, which is sure and stedfast (Heb 6:19). When the wicked one would beat down the soul with doubts of pardon or fears of falling, the helmet of salvation lifts the head, for the saint knows in whom he hath believed (2Ti 1:12). So the Scripture teaches that the mind kept by the hope of salvation is kept from the discouragement that disarms a soldier; the believer who wears this helmet looks beyond the battle to the certain victory God has promised, and being assured of the end, he fights the harder and faints not, for his salvation is of the Lord and cannot fail.
webster_summary: The fifth piece of the armour, the hope of salvation that guards the believer’s mind against doubt and discouragement.

etymology: From the Greek machaira, the short keen-edged sword of close combat, the sixth piece of the armour, figuring the word of God as the believer’s one weapon of offence.
biblical_def: The sword of the Spirit is the sixth and last piece of the whole armour of God, and the only weapon of offence among them: And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph 6:17). All the other pieces — girdle, breastplate, shoes, shield, helmet — are for defence, that the believer may stand and not be wounded; but the sword is the weapon by which he strikes at the enemy, and the apostle tells plainly what it is: the word of God. The dictionary marks this sword as the Scripture wielded by the believer in the power of the Holy Ghost who gave it; it is called the sword of the Spirit because the Spirit is its author and the Spirit makes it effectual in the saint’s hand. For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword (Heb 4:12); it cuts the conscience, slays the lie, and puts the tempter to flight. The Lord Himself, when tempted in the wilderness, wielded this very sword, answering the devil at every assault with It is written (Mat 4:4), and so vanquished him. So the Scripture teaches that the believer fights and conquers not by his own reasonings but by the written word rightly applied, the only weapon that can wound the powers of darkness. The saint who knows the Scriptures, and uses them as the Spirit teaches, holds a sword no temptation can withstand.
webster_summary: The sixth piece of the armour and the only weapon of offence, the word of God wielded by the Spirit who gave it.

etymology: From the Greek homologia, “a confession” or “an agreeing to say the same thing,” the believer’s open profession of Christ before men, after the pattern of Christ before Pilate.
biblical_def: The good confession is the believer’s open and faithful profession of the truth of Christ before men, named by the apostle Paul when he charged Timothy in the warfare of the gospel. Fight the good fight of faith, he writes, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses (1Ti 6:12). And he sets before Timothy the highest pattern of such confessing: Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate witnessed a good confession (1Ti 6:13). The dictionary marks the good confession as the soldier’s open avowal of his Captain — the confession of Christ the believer makes at his baptism, before the church, and before a watching and often hostile world. For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation (Rom 10:10), and Christ has bound the confessing of His name to His own confessing of us: whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven (Mat 10:32). So the Scripture teaches that faith does not hide but speaks; the believer who has laid hold on eternal life owns his Lord openly, as Christ owned the truth before Pilate though it cost Him His life. The good confession is faith come to speech, the open siding with Christ that marks the true soldier, to which the Lord has joined His promise to confess that soldier before His Father.

corruption_paragraphs: The good confession has drawn little redefinition, surviving as the apostle’s charge to Timothy in the fight of faith. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the open profession of Christ to which the believer is called, after the pattern of Christ before Pilate.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that true faith does not hide but speaks. With the heart man believeth unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation; and Christ has bound the confessing of His name to His own confessing of us before the Father. The believer who has laid hold on eternal life owns his Lord openly, as Christ witnessed a good confession before Pontius Pilate without flinching though it cost Him His life. So the good confession is faith come to speech, the open siding with Christ that marks the true soldier, to which the Lord has joined His promise to confess that soldier before His Father.

etymology: From the Greek karpos, “fruit” or “produce,” the graces the Holy Spirit brings forth in the believer, set against the works of the flesh.
biblical_def: The fruit of the Spirit is the cluster of graces the Holy Ghost brings forth in the believer, named by the apostle Paul in the epistle to the Galatians and set in direct contrast to the works of the flesh. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law (Gal 5:22, Gal 5:23). The dictionary marks the careful wording: the works of the flesh are many and called works, for the corrupt nature produces them of itself; but the fruit of the Spirit is one fruit, called fruit, for it is not the believer’s achievement but the produce of the Spirit dwelling in him, as fruit grows from a living tree. So the Scripture teaches that holiness is not the flesh refined but a new life implanted; the Spirit who regenerates the soul brings forth these graces as the increase of the new man. They who are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts (Gal 5:24). The fruit is borne not by striving in the strength of nature but by abiding in Christ, for He hath said, He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit; for without me ye can do nothing (Joh 15:5). This fruit is the evidence of regeneration and the appointed proof that a man has passed from the dominion of the flesh to the rule of the Spirit of God.

etymology: From the Greek thusia, “a sacrifice” or “offering,” the apostle’s figure for the believer’s whole self yielded up to God as an act of worship.
biblical_def: The living sacrifice is the apostle Paul’s figure for the entire dedication of the believer’s person to God, set at the head of the practical part of the epistle to the Romans. I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service (Rom 12:1). The dictionary marks the weight of the words. Under the law the sacrifice was a beast slain and consumed upon the altar; but the believer is bidden to offer a living sacrifice, not to die for God but to live wholly unto Him, his body and members given as instruments of righteousness. It is to be holy, set apart from sin; and acceptable, pleasing to God because offered through Christ. The apostle grounds the appeal not in fear but in the mercies of God — the mercies of election, redemption, justification, and adoption set forth before — so that the offering is the answer of a ransomed heart. This he calls the reasonable service, the worship that accords with reason once the mercies of God are known; for they who are bought with the precious blood of Christ should yield themselves wholly to Him. So the Scripture teaches that true worship is not a part of life set aside but the whole life laid on the altar; the believer is at once the priest and the offering, presenting himself a living sacrifice to the God who has redeemed him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that true worship is not a part of life set aside but the whole life laid on the altar. Under the law the sacrifice was a beast slain; but the believer is to present a living sacrifice, not dying for God but living wholly unto Him, his body and all its members given as instruments of righteousness. The offering is to be holy and acceptable through Christ, and it is grounded in the mercies of God, so that it is the answer of a ransomed and grateful heart.
